title: Extreme 2016 El Niño heatwave weakened carbon export and respiration in the Equatorial Pacific
abstract: The 2016 El Niño was the strongest warm-phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation recorded to date over the 21st century, leading to the development of severe ocean surface temperature anomalies - marine heatwaves - across the equatorial Pacific. Here we analyze biogeochemical model output and machine learning-based reconstructions of primarily Argo oxygen and backscattering measurements to demonstrate the impact of the 2016 El Niño in weakening oceanic carbon export - the transfer of biogenic carbon from the surface ocean to depth. We show that central equatorial Pacific anomalies in modeled carbon export flux and reconstructed optical particle backscatter and ecosystem respiration display interannual variations linked to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, with an acute reduction of 50 % in carbon export during the 2016 El Niño. This plunge in export production is attributed to a large decrease in chlorophyll biomass observed from space, and modeled ecological changes in phytoplankton community composition. The 2016 extreme El Niño led to near collapse of diatoms and reduction in carbon export and respiration, according to analyses of biogeochemical model output and machine learning based particle backscattering and oxygen fields.
problem: The biogeochemical and ecological impacts of extreme marine heatwaves on open ocean planktonic ecosystems are poorly understood and difficult to assess due to a lack of concurrent in-situ sensors to directly observe these changes as they happen.
method: This study combines a biogeochemical model with machine learning reconstructions of particle backscatter and oxygen utilization to demonstrate how the 2016 El Niño heatwave weakened oceanic carbon export and respiration in the Equatorial Pacific.
task: The task is to analyze the impact of the 2016 El Niño heatwave on oceanic carbon export and respiration in the Equatorial Pacific using a biogeochemical model and machine learning-based reconstructions of observational data.
innovation: This study combines a biogeochemical model with machine learning reconstructions of observational data to demonstrate that the extreme 2016 El Niño heatwave caused a significant weakening of carbon export and respiration in the equatorial Pacific, linking the event to changes in phytoplankton community composition.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Estimates of export production were obtained from the NASA Ocean Biogeochemical Model (NOBM). The NOBM is a coupled ocean-biogeochemical model that provides a three-dimensional representation of marine biogeochemical processes, guided by the assimilation of satellite ocean color at the surface layer. This version of the NOBM has a near-global domain spanning from 84°S to 72°N at a spatial resolution of 1° longitude and 2/3° latitude, and restricted to waters deeper than 200 m. The coupled circulation model is Poseidon79, a reduced gravity model with 14 vertical layers in quasi-isopycnal coordinates.

The model assimilates satellite ocean color retrievals of total surface chlorophyll, particulate inorganic carbon (PIC), and absorption by colored dissolved organic matter (aCDOM). The assimilation is conducted by minimizing the difference between the laplacian of the modeled surface fields and that of the satellite observations using the Conditional Relaxation Analysis Method (CRAM)82,83. Optical water properties are derived by the Ocean-Atmosphere Spectral Irradiance Model (OASIM)45. OASIM simulates the propagation of downward spectral irradiance in the atmosphere and ocean, and ultimately defines the level of photosynthetically available radiation (PAR) for phytoplankton growth.

The 2016 El Niño extended southward the oceanic area under heat stress previously initiated over the Northeast Pacific (Gulf of Alaska and the California Current System) by the “Blob” heatwave in 201315,16.

A recent biogeochemical reanalysis informed by the assimilation of space-based ocean color observations into an ocean ecological model (NASA Ocean Biogeochemical Model - NOBM) suggested major changes in phytoplankton community composition during the 2016 MHW in the Niño 3.4 region25 (5°S – 5°N, 170°W - 120°W, Figure 1).

El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the Earth’s strongest driver of interannual climate variability¹, leaving pronounced impacts on the biogeochemical conditions of the equatorial Pacific 2,3 and the global carbon budget 4,5,6.

ENSO appears to be a strong modulator of MHWs in both of it distinct phases, with El Niño leading to extreme warm anomalies in the central-to-eastern equatorial Pacific and Indian ocean, while La Niña is associated with strong MHWs in the subtropical south Pacific and extended regions of the temperate north and south Atlantic10.
